name: Attirampakkam Palaeolithic Site

kids: At Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu, archaeologists dug through deep layers of mud to find stone handaxes made 1.5 million years ago and smaller stone tools made over 300,000 years ago.
teen: Attirampakkam preserves a long Stone Age sequence in southern India: cosmogenic-nuclide dating places its Lower Palaeolithic Acheulian tools at c.
region: Kortallayar river basin, Tiruvallur district, Tamil Nadu

datings.label: Lower Palaeolithic Acheulian horizon (cosmogenic burial and paleomagnetic dating)
datings.note: Cosmogenic 26Al/10Be burial dating of laminated clays containing Acheulian handaxes and cleavers yields a pooled average age of 1.51 +/- 0.07 Ma within the Matuyama reversed chron (>1.07 Ma).

datings.label: Middle Palaeolithic transition (pIRIR luminescence dating)
datings.note: Post-infrared infrared stimulated luminescence (pIRIR) ages document the gradual loss of large cutting tools and the rise of Levallois core and point technology between c. 385 +/- 64 ka and 172 +/- 41 ka.

name: Bori Palaeolithic Site
summary: An open-air Acheulian locality on the Kukdi river in Pune district, Maharashtra, where early Acheulian trihedral picks, handaxes and flakes occur in gravels associated with a volcanic tephra layer whose age has been debated between early Middle Pleistocene Ar-Ar estimates and the c.
kids: At Bori in Maharashtra, archaeologists found ancient stone tools buried near layers of volcanic ash that drifted across the sea from a giant volcano in Indonesia.
teen: Bori in the Kukdi river valley yielded early Acheulian stone tools associated with volcanic ash; scientists have debated whether the ash dates the tools to around 670,000 years ago or represents reworked 75,000-year-old Toba tephra.
region: Kukdi river valley, Pune district, Maharashtra

datings.label: 39Ar-40Ar tephra dating hypothesis (Mishra et al. 1995)
datings.note: 39Ar-40Ar step-heating of magnetic mineral separates from the Bori tephra layer yielded a plateau age of 0.67 +/- 0.03 Ma for the associated early Acheulian industry.

datings.label: Youngest Toba Tuff geochemical correlation (Westgate et al. 1998)
datings.note: Glass-shard major- and trace-element chemistry and fission-track dates identify the Bori ash as the c. 75 ka Youngest Toba Tuff, indicating reworking of older Acheulian gravels and younger ash.

name: Earliest Known Cotton Fibres at Mehrgarh
summary: The earliest known archaeological evidence of cotton textile thread in the Old World, identified from mineralized Gossypium fibres preserved by copper corrosion products inside a biconical copper bead from a Period II burial at Neolithic Mehrgarh in Balochistan (c.
kids: Inside a tiny copper bead buried at Mehrgarh nearly 8,000 years ago, scientists using strong microscopes discovered preserved threads of cotton - the earliest known cotton string in the world.
teen: In 2002, archaeobotanists and metallurgists analyzing a copper bead from Period II at Mehrgarh identified mineralized spun cotton (Gossypium) thread dating to the 6th millennium BCE, pushing back the history of South Asian cotton use by over two thousand years.
region: Kachi Plain (Bolan River valley), Balochistan

datings.label: Period II Neolithic burial horizon at Mehrgarh (Moulherat et al. 2002)
datings.note: Recovered from Grave 153 in Structure 2 of Period II at Mound MR2, Mehrgarh, dated stratigraphically and radiometrically to the 6th millennium BCE.

name: Amri-Nal Phase
summary: An Early Harappan regional culture of lower Sindh, southern Balochistan and north Gujarat (c.
kids: In southern Sindh and the hills of Balochistan, early farmers and craftspeople of the Amri-Nal culture painted colourful geometric designs on fine clay bowls before the rise of Mohenjo-daro.
teen: The Amri-Nal phase represents the southern Regionalisation Era of the Indus tradition, linking seasonal highland settlements in Balochistan with year-round farming villages in the lower Indus plain and Gujarat.
region: Lower Sindh, Jhalawan (Balochistan), and Kutch-North Gujarat

datings.label: Early Harappan Amri-Nal Regionalisation Phase
datings.note: Stratified sequences at Amri (Periods IA-ID), Balakot, and Sohr Damb (Nal) date this southern Early Harappan horizon between the mid-4th millennium and c. 2600 BCE.

name: Kalibangan
summary: A major Early and Mature Harappan fortified town on the southern bank of the dry Ghaggar (ancient Sarasvati/Hakra) riverbed in Hanumangarh District, Rajasthan (c.
kids: At Kalibangan in Rajasthan, archaeologists uncovered a 4,800-year-old ploughed farm field with criss-cross furrows where farmers grew two crops at once.
teen: Excavated by B.
region: Hanumangarh District, Rajasthan, India

datings.label: Period I (Early Harappan Sothi-Siswal Occupation)
datings.note: Fortified mud-brick settlement using 1:2:3 ratio bricks and the furrowed agricultural field outside the southeastern wall; terminated by what the excavators identified as a seismic event around 2600 BCE.

datings.label: Period II (Mature Harappan Urban Occupation)
datings.note: Rebuilt on a bipartite plan with a fortified Western Citadel (KLB-1) and fortified Eastern Lower Town (KLB-2) using 1:2:4 Mature Harappan bricks, before abandonment around c. 1900 BCE as the Ghaggar dried.

name: Kalibangan Early Harappan Ploughed Field
summary: An in situ furrowed agricultural horizon excavated outside the southeastern fortification wall of Early Harappan (Period I, c.
kids: Buried under later town layers at Kalibangan in Rajasthan is an ancient farm field with two sets of plough lines crossing each other so farmers could grow two crops at the same time.
teen: Dated to c.
region: Kalibangan, Hanumangarh District, Rajasthan, India

datings.label: Kalibangan Period I (Early Harappan Sothi-Siswal Horizon)
datings.note: Sealed directly beneath Mature Harappan Period II deposits outside the southeastern corner of the Early Harappan Period I fortification at Kalibangan.

name: Harappan Steatite Stamp Seals
summary: Over 3,700 carved and alkali-fired square and rectangular steatite stamp seals and moulded tablets produced across the Harappan Civilisation (primarily c.
kids: Harappan merchants and officials carved small square stone seals with animals like the unicorn, zebu bull, and elephant, and pressed them into wet clay to seal packages of trade goods.
teen: Carved in soft steatite and whitened by kiln firing, more than 3,700 Harappan stamp seals functioned as tokens of authority, clan identity, and commercial certification across the Indus basin and as far away as Mesopotamia.
region: Pan-Harappan (with exports found in the Persian Gulf, Susa, Ur, Kish, and Nippur)

datings.label: Early Kot Dijian Origins (c. 2800-2600 BCE) and Mature Harappan Standardisation (c. 2600-1900 BCE)
datings.note: Early geometric and animal stamp seals appear in Harappa Period 2 (c. 2800-2600 BCE), reaching full standardisation with script and perforated boss backs during Period 3A-3C (c. 2600-1900 BCE).

name: Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro
summary: A 10.5-centimetre solid bronze statuette cast by the lost-wax (cire perdue) technique during the Mature Harappan period (c.
kids: The Dancing Girl is a small bronze statue from Mohenjo-daro, just over ten centimetres tall, showing a confident young woman wearing more than twenty shell bangles on her left arm.
teen: Excavated in Mohenjo-daro's HR Area in 1926 and now housed in the National Museum, New Delhi, the Dancing Girl demonstrates Mature Harappan mastery of lost-wax bronze casting and naturalistic figural sculpture.
region: Mohenjo-daro, Sindh (housed in the National Museum, New Delhi)

datings.label: Mature Harappan Context at Mohenjo-daro (HR Area)
datings.note: Excavated by Daya Ram Sahni and Ernest Mackay in 1926 from a Mature Harappan house in the southern HR Area of Mohenjo-daro.

name: Dholavira Signboard
summary: A unique Mature Harappan monumental inscription found in the western chamber of the North Gate of the Castle at Dholavira, Gujarat (c.
kids: Above the northern castle gate at Dholavira once hung a giant wooden board inlaid with ten gleaming white mineral letters so large they could be seen from far across the city.
teen: Excavated in the northern gateway of Dholavira's Castle by R.
region: Dholavira, Kutch District, Gujarat, India

datings.label: Mature Harappan Stage IV-V Context at Dholavira
datings.note: Found lying in the western chamber of the North Gate of the Castle; the ASI nomination dossier places the inscription in use during Stage IV, the classical Mature Harappan stage at Dholavira.

name: Ganweriwala
summary: A large Mature Harappan urban centre in the Cholistan desert of Bahawalpur, Punjab, Pakistan, situated along the dry bed of the Hakra River roughly equidistant between Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, surveyed by M.
kids: Deep in the Cholistan desert of Pakistan lies Ganweriwala, a major Harappan city along the dry Hakra riverbed halfway between Mohenjo-daro and Harappa.
teen: Documented by M.
region: Cholistan Desert, Bahawalpur District, Punjab, Pakistan

datings.label: Mature Harappan Urban Centre in Cholistan
datings.note: Dated by surface ceramic assemblages, baked bricks in 1:2:4 proportions, terracotta cakes, and an impressed clay tablet to the Mature Harappan Integration Era (c. 2600-1900 BCE).

name: Mohenjo-daro
summary: The largest excavated Mature Harappan metropolis (over 200 hectares), situated on the right bank of the Indus River in Larkana District, Sindh, renowned for its elevated mud-brick citadel platform, the Great Bath, massive brick drains, hundreds of deep brick-lined wells, and famous bronze and steatite sculptures.
kids: Mohenjo-daro was a huge brick city built along the Indus River around 2500 BCE, with two-storey houses, private wells, bathrooms, covered street drains, and the famous Great Bath.
teen: Excavated from 1922 onward by R.
region: Larkana District, Sindh, Pakistan

datings.label: Mature Harappan Urban Occupation
datings.note: Major urban construction and occupation belong to the Mature Harappan Integration Era (c. 2600-1900 BCE), with unexcavated Early Harappan levels submerged beneath the modern water table and a brief Late Harappan Jhukar-related occupation in the uppermost strata.

name: Sutkagen-dor
summary: The westernmost known fortified coastal outpost of the Mature Harappan Civilisation, situated on the eastern bank of the Dasht River along the Makran coast of southwestern Balochistan near the Pakistan-Iran border (c.
kids: Sutkagen-dor was a stone-walled Harappan fortress near the Arabian Sea coast on the edge of modern Pakistan and Iran, where ships stopped on their way to Oman and Mesopotamia.
teen: Investigated by Aurel Stein and George Dales in the Dasht valley of Balochistan, Sutkagen-dor marks the western coastal frontier of the Mature Harappan world, built with stone walls up to 9 metres thick at the base to guard maritime trade routes along the Makran coast.
region: Makran Coast, Gwadar District, Balochistan, Pakistan

datings.label: Mature Harappan Coastal Outpost
datings.note: Dated by diagnostic Mature Harappan black-on-red ceramics, shell bangles, copper-bronze blades, and stone masonry architecture examined by Aurel Stein (1928) and George F. Dales (1960).

name: Lothal
summary: A compact Mature and Late Harappan manufacturing and trading town near the Gulf of Khambhat in Gujarat (c.
kids: Lothal was a busy Harappan craft and trade town in Gujarat with a bead workshop, a storehouse full of stamped clay tags, and a giant brick-lined water basin.
teen: Excavated by S.
region: Bhal region, Ahmedabad District, Gujarat, India

datings.label: Lothal Period A (Mature Harappan Phases I to IV)
datings.note: Calibrated radiocarbon dates place the planned urban trading settlement of Lothal A between c. 2400 and 1900 BCE.

datings.label: Lothal Period B (Late Harappan Phase V)
datings.note: Post-urban Late Sorath / Rangpur IIB-IIC occupation following severe flood damage around 1900 BCE.

name: The 4.2 ka Aridification Event and Monsoon Weakening in Northwest India
summary: A major multi-century palaeoclimatic shift commencing around 4,200 to 4,100 years ago (c.
kids: Around 2200 to 2100 BCE, the summer monsoon rains in northwestern India grew much weaker for several centuries, drying up seasonal rivers and ponds that Harappan farmers relied on.
teen: Documented in oxygen-isotope records from Lake Kotla Dahar in Haryana (Dixit et al.
region: Northwestern Indian Subcontinent (Indus and Ghaggar-Hakra basins, Haryana, Rajasthan, Gujarat)

datings.label: Abrupt Summer Monsoon Weakening at Kotla Dahar (~4.1 ka BP) and 4.2 ka Event
datings.note: Anchored by radiocarbon-dated gastropod shell oxygen-isotope (delta-18O) shifts at paleolake Kotla Dahar in Haryana (~4,100 cal yr BP, c. 2150 BCE; Dixit et al. 2014), marine cores off the Indus delta, and bioapatite records at Bhirrana (Sarkar et al. 2016).

name: Sarasvati in the Rigveda
summary: In the Rigveda, Sarasvati is celebrated both as a mighty, snow-fed river flowing from the mountains to the sea (or terminal lake) and as the goddess of sacred speech and ritual inspiration.
kids: In the Rigveda, the Sarasvati is praised as a grand river flowing from the mountains and as a goddess of wisdom.
teen: Positioned explicitly between the Yamuna and the Shutudri (Sutlej) in the Nadistuti hymn (Rigveda 10.75.5), the Rigvedic Sarasvati corresponds geographically to the Ghaggar-Hakra system, while geologists and historians debate when it transitioned from a perennial to a monsoon-fed seasonal river.
region: Kurukshetra and Ghaggar-Hakra basin (Haryana, Punjab, northern Rajasthan, and Cholistan)

datings.label: Fluvial geomorphology of the Ghaggar-Hakra monsoonal decline (Giosan et al. 2012)
datings.note: Fluvial geomorphology and luminescence dating by Liviu Giosan et al. (2012) indicate that during the Holocene Harappan phase the Ghaggar-Hakra was a perennial monsoon-fed system whose discharges weakened after c. 2000 to 1900 BCE as the summer monsoon aridified.

datings.label: Rigvedic to Brahmana textual hydrology (Witzel, Jamison and Brereton)
datings.note:
In the Rigveda (c. 1500 to 1000 BCE in mainstream chronology) the Sarasvati is described as a swollen river, whereas by the Panchavimsha and Jaiminiya Brahmanas (c. 900 to 700 BCE) it is
 explicitly described as disappearing into the desert at Vinashana.

datings.label: Pre-1900 BCE glacial-fed Sarasvati correlation (Danino, Lal)
datings.note: Michel Danino and B. B. Lal argue that Rigvedic descriptions of the Sarasvati breaking mountain ridges and flowing from the mountains to the ocean (RV 7.95.2) must predate the late Harappan drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra around 1900 BCE.

name: Sanauli (Sinauli)
summary: A major Bronze Age necropolis in Baghpat District, western Uttar Pradesh, in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab (c.
kids: At Sanauli in Uttar Pradesh, archaeologists uncovered 4,000-year-old warrior burials with wooden coffins, copper swords, and two-wheeled wooden vehicles decorated with copper triangles.
teen: Excavated by the ASI in 2005-2006 and 2018, the Sanauli cemetery in western Uttar Pradesh yielded elite warrior graves with copper weapons and solid-wheeled two-wheeled vehicles dated to c.
region: Baghpat District, western Uttar Pradesh, India (Yamuna-Hindon interfluve)

datings.label: Radiocarbon and Thermoluminescence Dates of the Sanauli Cemeteries (2005 and 2018)
datings.note: Calibrated AMS radiocarbon dates on organic material from the 2018 ASI excavations and luminescence dates from the 2005-2006 cemetery cluster between c. 2200/2100 and 1800 BCE.

name: Jhukar Phase (Sindh Late Harappan)
summary: The Late Harappan regional phase of Sindh (c.
kids: As the big cities of Sindh grew smaller after 1900 BCE, people in the Jhukar phase stopped using the Indus script and made round clay and stone button seals instead.
teen: The Jhukar phase marks the post-urban Late Harappan period in Sindh (c.
region: Middle and Lower Indus valley (Sindh, Pakistan)

datings.label: Sindh Late Harappan (Localisation Era)
datings.note: Stratigraphically overlies Mature Harappan levels at Chanhudaro II, Jhukar, and Amri IIID, and precedes the Jhangar phase.

name: Daimabad Chalcolithic Site and Bronzes
summary: The largest Chalcolithic settlement in the Godavari-Pravara basin of Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra (c.
kids: At Daimabad in Maharashtra, a farmer unearthed four heavy bronze sculptures on wheels - an elephant, a rhino, a buffalo and a two-bull chariot driven by a man with a dog - made in the Late Harappan and Chalcolithic era.
teen: Excavated by M.
region: Pravara River valley (Godavari basin), Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra

datings.label: Five-phase Chalcolithic radiocarbon and stratigraphic sequence
datings.note: Stratigraphy and radiocarbon dates span Phase I Savalda (c. 2200-2000 BCE), Phase II Late Harappan (c. 2000-1800 BCE), Phase III Daimabad ware (c. 1800-1600 BCE), Phase IV Malwa (c. 1600-1400 BCE) and Phase V Jorwe (c. 1400-1000 BCE).

name: Paiyampalli Neolithic and Megalithic Site
summary: A stratified terrace settlement at the foot of the Talathapamalai hills in Tirupattur (formerly North Arcot) district, Tamil Nadu, excavated by S.
kids: At Paiyampalli in Tamil Nadu, ancient farmers lived on hill terraces in round huts and dwelling pits, grew pulses and millets, and later learned to smelt iron and build stone megalithic tombs.
teen: Excavated by S.
region: Palar-Ponnaiyar watershed, Tirupattur district, Tamil Nadu

datings.label: Radiocarbon dates for Period I Neolithic and Period II Megalithic levels
datings.note: Calibrated charcoal radiocarbon dates place Period I (Neolithic) at c. 1800-1300 BCE and Period II (Megalithic with Black-and-Red Ware and iron slag) from the late 2nd to mid-1st millennium BCE.

name: Hittite-Mitanni Treaty of Suppiluliuma I and Shattiwaza
summary: The cuneiform treaty concluded around 1380 BCE between the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I and the Mitanni prince Shattiwaza (Kurtiwaza), discovered at Hattusa (Bogazkoy), invokes four Vedic deities - Mitra, Varuna, Indra, and the Nasatyas (Ashvins) - as divine witnesses.
kids: Around 1380 BCE, two ancient kings in West Asia signed a clay-tablet peace treaty that called upon four Vedic gods - Mitra, Varuna, Indra, and the Nasatyas - as witnesses.
teen: Excavated on cuneiform tablets at the Hittite capital of Hattusa, the c.
region: Upper Mesopotamia and Anatolia (found at Hattusa, modern Bogazkale, Turkey)

datings.label: Reign of Suppiluliuma I of Hatti (Hattusa cuneiform archive)
datings.note: Directly attested on Akkadian cuneiform tablets from the royal archives of Hattusa dated to the reign of Suppiluliuma I (c. 1380 to 1346 BCE).

name: Kurukshetra War
summary: The Kurukshetra War is the eighteen-day dynastic conflict between the Pandavas and Kauravas of the Kuru lineage narrated at the centre of the Mahabharata.
kids: The Kurukshetra War is the famous eighteen-day battle between the Pandavas and Kauravas described in the Mahabharata, whose date is debated between ancient tradition and modern historians.
teen: The Kurukshetra War of the Mahabharata has no direct contemporary inscription or secure archaeological horizon: historians place any underlying Kuru conflict in the early Iron Age (c.
region: Kurukshetra (Haryana) and the Kuru-Panchala Doab

datings.label: Early Iron Age Kuru-Panchala and Painted Grey Ware horizon (B. B. Lal and mainstream historians)
datings.note: Associates a possible historical kernel of an intra-Kuru conflict with the Vedic Kuru-Panchala polity and Painted Grey Ware sites (Hastinapura, Indraprastha, Ahichchhatra, Kurukshetra) of c. 1200-800 BCE, while noting that archaeology cannot verify the epic war itself.

datings.label: Aryabhata and Aihole inscription Kali Yuga epoch (3102 BCE)
datings.note: The 634 CE Aihole inscription of Pulakeshin II equates Saka 556 with 3,735 years elapsed since the Bharata war, matching Aryabhata's 3102 BCE Kali Yuga epoch.

datings.label: Puranic and Brihat Samhita traditional reckonings (3138 BCE and 2449 BCE)
datings.note: One traditional reckoning places the war 36 years before the 3102 BCE Kali Yuga onset (3138/3139 BCE), while another preserved by Varahamihira (Brihat Samhita 13.3) and Kalhana places Yudhishthira 653 years into the Kali Yuga (2449 BCE).

datings.label: Planetarium-software reconstructions (B. N. Narahari Achar 3067 BCE; competing 1793 and 1478 BCE models)
datings.note: B. N. Narahari Achar simulated planetary and eclipse notices in the Udyogaparvan and Bhishmaparvan with planetarium software to propose 3067 BCE (building on S. Balakrishna and K. S. Raghavan), whereas other authors using different subsets of the same verses propose 1478 BCE or 1793 BCE; Indologists and historians of astronomy regard these reconstructions as speculative because the epic's astronomical verses are poetic, multi-layered and mutually contradictory.

name: Hastinapura (Hastinapur)
summary: Hastinapura, located on an old bank of the Ganga in Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh, is the traditional capital of the Kuru kingdom and a benchmark site of North Indian protohistoric archaeology.
kids: Hastinapura is an ancient city by the Ganga River that served as the capital of the Kuru kingdom.
teen: Excavated by B.
region: Upper Ganga-Yamuna Doab (Meerut district, western Uttar Pradesh)

datings.label: Stratified protohistoric and early historic sequence (Periods I to III, B. B. Lal)
datings.note: B. B. Lal identified Period I (Ochre Coloured Pottery, pre-1200 BCE), Period II (Painted Grey Ware, dated by Lal to c. 1100 to 800 BCE), and Period III (Northern Black Polished Ware, c. 6th to 3rd century BCE), followed by later historical occupations in Periods IV and V.

name: Gautama Buddha
summary: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha ("the Awakened One"), was a teacher of the Shakya clan, born at Lumbini, whose teaching of the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path is the foundation of Buddhism.
kids: Siddhartha Gautama was born at Lumbini in the Shakya clan.
teen: The Buddha taught in the middle Gangetic plain.
region: Middle Gangetic plain and Nepal Terai (Lumbini, Bodh Gaya, Sarnath, Kushinagar)

datings.label: Corrected long chronology (lifespan)
datings.note: The Sri Lankan chronicles place Ashoka's consecration 218 years after the Parinirvana; counted from a consecration of about 268 BCE this gives a death around 486 to 483 BCE and, with an 80-year life, a birth around 566 to 563 BCE. Long favoured by Wilhelm Geiger and many historians of India.

datings.label: Short chronology (lifespan; Heinz Bechert, Richard Gombrich and others)
datings.note: Northern Buddhist traditions put Ashoka about a century after the Parinirvana, and the Vinaya lists of teachers are too short for a 218-year gap; scholars at the Gottingen symposium edited by Heinz Bechert therefore place the death around 420 to 380 BCE. Cousins reviews these arguments.

datings.label: Theravada Buddhist Era
datings.note: The Buddhist Era used in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia places the Parinirvana in 544 or 543 BCE, after an 80-year life.

name: Mahavira
summary: Vardhamana Mahavira is revered in Jainism as the twenty-fourth and last Tirthankara of the present age.
kids: Mahavira was the twenty-fourth great teacher, or Tirthankara, of Jainism.
teen: Mahavira, a contemporary of the Buddha, taught in Bihar and organised the Jain community of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen.
region: Middle Gangetic plain (Vaishali and Pava, Bihar)

datings.label: Scholarly dating as a contemporary of the Buddha (lifespan)
datings.note: Pali texts say that Nigantha Nataputta (Mahavira) died at Pava while the Buddha was still alive, so his dates follow the Buddha's; with the now widely preferred later date for the Buddha, his death falls in the 5th century BCE.

datings.label: Traditional Vira Nirvana era
datings.note: The Vira Nirvana Samvat, the era counted from Mahavira's liberation, places his death in 527 BCE after a life of 72 years.

name: Major Rock Edict XIII of Ashoka
summary: Major Rock Edict XIII is Ashoka's inscription on the conquest of Kalinga in his eighth regnal year and his remorse for its suffering, with a Greek adaptation at Kandahar.
kids: After a terrible war in Kalinga, Emperor Ashoka carved a message in stone saying he was deeply sorry for the suffering and would now try to win people over through dharma instead of war.
teen: Edict XIII records Ashoka's remorse over the Kalinga war and names five Greek kings whose dates are known from Greek records.
region: Pan-Indian (versions at Kalsi, Shahbazgarhi, Mansehra, Girnar, Erragudi and elsewhere; Greek adaptation at Kandahar)

datings.label: Synchronism with five Hellenistic kings
datings.note: All five kings were reigning together only between the accession of Antiochus II (261 BCE) and the death of Magas of Cyrene, placed by different scholars around 258 or 250 BCE; the identity of Alikasudara (Alexander of Epirus or of Corinth) also affects the lower limit.

name: Maurya Empire
summary: The Maurya Empire (about 322 to 185 BCE), founded by Chandragupta Maurya with its capital at Pataliputra, is the earliest known state to rule most of the Indian subcontinent together with parts of present-day Afghanistan.
kids: The Maurya Empire united most of the Indian subcontinent about 2,300 years ago.
teen: From about 322 to 185 BCE the Maurya Empire joined northern, western and much of peninsular India under one government.
region: Most of the Indian subcontinent and eastern Afghanistan (from Kandahar to Bengal and Karnataka)

datings.label: Mainstream chronology (about 322 to 185 BCE)
datings.note: Anchored by Greek synchronisms for Chandragupta (Sandrokottos) and Ashoka (Major Rock Edict XIII), with the total dynastic length of 137 years given in the Puranas.

name: Ashoka
summary: Ashoka, who called himself Devanampiya Piyadasi ("Beloved of the Gods, of gracious mien"), was the third Maurya emperor and reigned from about 268 to 232 BCE.
kids: Emperor Ashoka ruled the Maurya Empire.
teen: Ashoka, reigning about 268 to 232 BCE, is the earliest known Indian ruler whose own inscriptions survive.
region: Most of the Indian subcontinent (capital at Pataliputra)

datings.label: Reign (about 268 to 232 BCE)
datings.note: The Hellenistic kings named in Major Rock Edict XIII put his consecration around 268 BCE; Buddhist chronicles place his accession a few years earlier, and the reign lengths of 36 or 37 years in Indian sources end it around 232 BCE.

name: Rama
summary: Rama, son of Dasharatha, prince of Ayodhya in the Ikshvaku (Solar) line and hero of the Valmiki Ramayana, is revered in Hindu tradition as an avatar of Vishnu and the model of dharma.
kids: Rama, the prince of Ayodhya and hero of the Ramayana, is honoured in Hindu tradition as an avatar of Vishnu who stood for truth and duty.
teen: Traditional chronology places Rama in the Treta Yuga, long before the Mahabharata.
region: Kosala (Ayodhya) and the wider subcontinent in epic geography

datings.label: Traditional placement in the Treta Yuga (Treta of the current mahayuga)
datings.note: The epic and Puranic tradition places Rama in a Treta Yuga; this range is the Treta of the present (28th) mahayuga in the standard 4:3:2:1 scheme. Other reckonings place him at the Treta-Dvapara junction or in the Treta of an earlier mahayuga.

datings.label: Composition of the Valmiki Ramayana (date of the text; Goldman, Brockington)
datings.note: Goldman places the core of the poem (Books 2 to 6) as early as about 750-500 BCE and Brockington somewhat later; both regard the Balakanda and Uttarakanda as additions of roughly the last centuries BCE to the early centuries CE.

name: Shunga Dynasty
summary: The Shunga dynasty (c.
kids: After the Maurya Empire ended around 185 BCE, the Shunga dynasty ruled northern and central India from Pataliputra and Vidisha for over a century.
teen: Founded by Pushyamitra Shunga around 185 BCE, the Shunga dynasty defended the Gangetic plain against Indo-Greek incursions, patronised Vedic ritual, and oversaw the stone expansion of Buddhist stupas at Bharhut and Sanchi.
region: Gangetic plain and Malwa (Pataliputra and Vidisha)

datings.label: Post-Mauryan Shunga rule (c. 185-73 BCE)
datings.note: Anchored by the end of the Maurya dynasty c. 185 BCE, Puranic king lists assigning ten Shunga kings 112 years before the Kanva coup, and the c. 113 BCE Heliodorus pillar synchronism at Vidisha.

name: Krishna
summary: Krishna Vasudeva of the Vrishni clan is a central figure of the Mahabharata, the teacher of the Bhagavadgita and, across Hindu traditions, an avatar of Vishnu or the supreme deity.
kids: Krishna is a hero and teacher of the Mahabharata and the Bhagavadgita, worshipped by millions.
teen: Tradition places Krishna at the Dvapara-Kali transition, in 3102 BCE or, in another school, around 2449 BCE.
region: Mathura (Shurasena), Kurukshetra and Dvaraka in epic geography

datings.label: Puranic-Siddhantic tradition (war 3138 BCE, passing at the start of Kali Yuga, 3102 BCE)
datings.note: The Vishnu Purana (4.24, 5.38) says Kali Yuga began on the day Krishna left the world, 36 years after the war; equated with the Siddhantic Kali epoch, this places his passing in 3102 BCE and the war in 3138 BCE.

datings.label: Vriddha Garga, Varahamihira and Kalhana school (Yudhishthira 2449 BCE)
datings.note: Varahamihira, quoted by Kalhana (Rajatarangini 1.56), dates Yudhishthira's reign to 2,526 years before the Shaka era (2449 BCE); Krishna, his contemporary, would then belong to the mid-25th century BCE.

datings.label: Krishna Devakiputra in Chandogya Upanishad 3.17.6 (date of the text; identification debated)
datings.note: The Chandogya Upanishad, dated by Olivelle to roughly the 7th to 6th centuries BCE, names Krishna son of Devaki as a pupil of Ghora Angirasa; whether he is the Krishna of the epic is debated.

datings.label: Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar, worship of Vasudeva (date by the reign of Antialcidas)
datings.note: Heliodorus, envoy of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas and a self-described Bhagavata, set up a Garuda column for Vasudeva, god of gods; the date follows the approximate reign of Antialcidas.

name: Vikram Samvat Era (57 BCE)
summary: Vikram Samvat is one of the main historical and civil eras of northern and western India and Nepal, counting luni-solar years from an epoch in 58-57 BCE.
kids: Vikram Samvat is a traditional Indian calendar that starts in 57 BCE, so its year number is about 57 more than the common calendar.
teen: The era of 57 BCE appears in 3rd to 5th century inscriptions from Rajasthan and Malwa as the Krita and then the Malava era.
region: Northern, western and central India, and Nepal

datings.label: Epoch of the Krita, Malava or Vikrama era fixed by dated inscriptions
datings.note: Synchronisms in dated inscriptions place year 1 of the era in 58-57 BCE; years beginning in the spring month Chaitra start in 57 BCE, those beginning in the autumn month Kartika in 58 BCE.

datings.label: Traditional foundation by King Vikramaditya of Ujjain
datings.note: Later literary and Jain tradition, including the story of Kalakacharya, credits the era to a king Vikramaditya of Ujjayini who expelled the Shakas.

name: Tamil-Brahmi Inscriptions
summary: Tamil-Brahmi (also called Tamili) inscriptions are the earliest known inscriptions in Tamil, and among the earliest in any Dravidian language, adapted from the Brahmi script with special graphemes (ḻ, ṟ, ṇ, ṉ) and orthographical conventions for Tamil phonology.
kids: Tamil-Brahmi (Tamili) inscriptions are ancient Tamil writings carved into rock caves and scratched onto clay pots, showing that people in South India were writing Tamil more than 2,000 years ago.
teen: Adapted from Brahmi by adding letters unique to Tamil speech, Tamil-Brahmi cave inscriptions and inscribed potsherds are the oldest written Tamil.
region: Tamilakam (Tamil Nadu and Kerala), with trade finds at Anuradhapura, Berenike and Quseir al-Qadim

datings.label: Palaeographic chronology (mainstream epigraphy)
datings.note: On letter forms, the cave inscriptions are usually dated from the late 3rd or 2nd century BCE, after Ashokan Brahmi, to the 3rd or 4th century CE, when Vatteluttu replaces them. Coningham and colleagues' pre-Ashokan Brahmi dates from Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka are the main challenge to a purely Mauryan origin for southern Brahmi.

datings.label: Pre-Ashokan potsherd radiocarbon dates proposed from Kodumanal, Porunthal and Keezhadi
datings.note: Radiocarbon dates from charcoal and paddy in strata yielding Tamil-Brahmi inscribed potsherds at Porunthal, Kodumanal and Keezhadi (down to c. 580 BCE) have prompted K. Rajan and the Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology to argue for a pre-Ashokan fifth- or sixth-century BCE origin, while other epigraphists await direct AMS dating of the inscribed sherds and scrutinize stratigraphic mixing.

name: Shaka Era (78 CE)
summary: The Shaka era is a continuous Indian era whose year 1 began in the spring of 78 CE.
kids: The Shaka era is an Indian way of counting years that starts in 78 CE.
teen: Counting from 78 CE, the Shaka era was used by the Western Kshatrapa rulers, then by astronomers and in inscriptions across the Deccan, South India and Southeast Asia.
region: Western India, the Deccan, South India and Southeast Asia; now India's national calendar

datings.label: Epoch of the Shaka era fixed by dated records (78 CE)
datings.note: Synchronisms in dated inscriptions and astronomical works, such as the Aihole inscription's equation of Shaka 556 with Kali 3735, fix the epoch of Shaka year 1 in the spring of 78 CE.

datings.label: Later Deccan attribution to King Shalivahana
datings.note: In medieval inscriptions and almanacs the era came to be called Shalivahana-shaka, crediting its start to a king Shalivahana, usually identified in tradition with the Satavahana line.

name: Mathura Art
summary: The Mathura school of sculpture was an indigenous Indian artistic tradition centred at Mathura on the Yamuna River in Uttar Pradesh, carved in distinctive buff-spotted Sikri red sandstone from roughly the second century BCE through the Kushan and Gupta periods.
kids: Carved from spotted red sandstone along the Yamuna River, the Mathura school of art created early statues of the Buddha, Jain Tirthankaras and Hindu deities.
teen: Working in distinctive Sikri spotted red sandstone from c.
region: Braj region along the Yamuna River (Mathura, Uttar Pradesh)

datings.label: Epigraphically dated Mathura sandstone sculpture from Shunga/Mitra through Shaka, Kushan and Gupta eras
datings.note: Anchored by dated inscriptions from the reign of the Northern Kshatrapa Sodasa (early first century CE) and the Kanishka-era pedestals of Friar Bala (Year 3 of Kanishka = c. 129 CE) through Gupta-dated Buddha and Jina images.

name: Gupta Empire
summary: The Gupta Empire (c.
kids: The Gupta Empire ruled northern India from around 319 to 550 CE, a period famous for great poets like Kalidasa, mathematician-astronomers like Aryabhata, the Iron Pillar of Delhi and the founding of Nalanda University.
teen: Inaugurating the Gupta calendar era in 319/320 CE and reaching its territorial peak under Samudragupta and Chandragupta II, the Gupta Empire presided over the classical standardization of Sanskrit literature, Hindu temple iconography, Buddhist monastic universities and mathematical astronomy.
region: Northern, Eastern, Central and Western India (capitals at Pataliputra, Ayodhya and Ujjain)

datings.label: Imperial Gupta Era chronology (Epoch 319/320 CE to Year 224 = 543/544 CE Damodarpur plate)
datings.note: Anchored by the epoch of the Gupta era (319-320 CE) determined from Al-Biruni and the Mandasor, Udayagiri, Sanchi, Eran and Damodarpur inscriptions spanning Gupta Year 61 (380 CE) to Year 224 (543/544 CE).

name: Kali Yuga Epoch (18 February 3102 BCE)
summary: In traditional Siddhantic astronomy the present Kali Yuga began at 17-18 February 3102 BCE (Julian), the zero point from which Indian astronomers counted planetary motion and the Kali era.
kids: Indian astronomers and traditional calendars say the present Kali Yuga began on 18 February 3102 BCE, and they counted years and planet positions from that day.
teen: Aryabhata wrote that 3,600 years of the present age had passed when he was 23, which places the start of Kali Yuga in 3102 BCE.
region: Pan-Indian (Ujjain as the prime meridian of Siddhantic astronomy)

datings.label: Siddhantic epoch of Kali Yuga (17-18 February 3102 BCE)
datings.note: The Surya Siddhanta and Aryabhata's midnight (ardharatrika) system place the epoch at midnight at Ujjain ending 17 February 3102 BCE (Julian); the Aryabhatiya's sunrise (audayika) system places it at mean sunrise on 18 February.

datings.label: Earliest known statement of the epoch, Aryabhatiya Kalakriyapada 10 (499 CE)
datings.note: Aryabhata states that when 3,600 years and three yuga-quarters had elapsed he was 23 years old; Kali year 3600 corresponds to Shaka 421, that is 499 CE.

name: Aihole inscription
summary: The Aihole inscription is a Sanskrit praise-poem (prashasti) by the Jain poet Ravikirti, carved on the Meguti temple at Aihole and dated Shaka 556 (634 to 635 CE).
kids: On a temple wall at Aihole in Karnataka, a poet carved a long poem in Sanskrit praising King Pulakeshin II.
teen: The Aihole inscription is a historian's gift: it is dated, it describes real wars, including Pulakeshin II's defeat of Harsha, and its poet invokes Kalidasa and Bharavi as literary comparators.
region: Bagalkot district, Karnataka

datings.label: Dated Shaka 556
datings.note: The inscription gives both Shaka 556 and 3,735 years after the Bharata war.

name: Kailasa Temple, Ellora
summary: The Kailasa temple (Cave 16) at Ellora is a complete Shiva temple carved downwards out of the basalt hillside, with its shrine, halls, courtyard and free-standing columns all cut from the living rock.
kids: The Kailasa temple was not built from blocks.
teen: Instead of stacking stones, carvers at Ellora removed rock around a block of hillside and shaped the block into a two-storey temple with sculpture everywhere.
region: Aurangabad district, Maharashtra

datings.label: Reign of Krishna I and after
datings.note: A later Rashtrakuta copper-plate grant praises Krishna I's temple at Elapura; work on the complex may have continued after him.

name: Adi Shankara
summary: Shankara (Shankaracharya) is the most influential teacher of Advaita Vedanta, known through his commentaries on the Brahmasutras, the principal Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita.
kids: Shankara was a teacher from Kerala who taught that the deepest self in every person is the same as Brahman, the one reality behind everything.
teen: Shankara's commentaries explain Advaita, non-dualism: the self (atman) is identical with Brahman, and the world of many things is not ultimately real.
region: Born at Kalady, Kerala, according to tradition; active across India

datings.label: Mainstream scholarly date (conventional 788 to 820 CE)
datings.note: Based on his references to earlier thinkers and later authors who cite him; several scholars prefer a slightly earlier date in the first half of the 8th century.

datings.label: Kanchi and Dwaraka matha tradition
datings.note: The succession lists of these mathas count back to a founder born in 509 BCE who lived thirty-two years.

name: Rajendra Chola I
summary: Rajendra I, son of Rajaraja I, ruled the Chola empire from 1014 to 1044 CE.
kids: Rajendra was a Chola king who sent his army all the way north to the river Ganga and his navy across the sea to the islands of Southeast Asia.
teen: Rajendra built on his father's empire.
region: Tamil Nadu

datings.label: Reign
datings.note: He was associated with his father as heir from about 1012 CE.

name: Ramanuja
summary: Ramanuja was the principal teacher of Vishishtadvaita Vedanta and of the Shrivaishnava community centred on the Srirangam temple.
kids: Ramanuja was a teacher who said that God is like a soul and the whole world is like God's body.
teen: Against Shankara's view that the world of many things is not ultimately real, Ramanuja argued that souls and matter are real but depend on God, as a body depends on its self.
region: Tamil Nadu (born at Sriperumbudur by tradition; active at Srirangam)

datings.label: Scholarly placement in the 11th to 12th centuries
datings.note: Scholars accept the 11th to 12th century setting; some regard the traditional 120-year life as idealised.

datings.label: Shrivaishnava tradition
datings.note: The hagiographies give a lifespan of 120 years.

name: Saptarishi Calendar (Laukika Era)
summary: The Saptarishi or Laukika era is a reckoning long used in Kashmir and the neighbouring hills.
kids: The Saptarishi calendar is a traditional calendar from Kashmir.
teen: Kashmiri Brahmans still keep the Laukika or Saptarishi era, whose traditional start is 25 years after the 3102 BCE Kali epoch.
region: Kashmir and the western Himalayan hill states (Chamba, Kangra, Mandi)

datings.label: Traditional Kashmiri epoch of the Laukika era
datings.note: Kashmiri Brahman tradition, first brought to European notice by Georg Buhler, places the start of the Laukika era on Chaitra shukla 1 of Kali year 25 expired, the year 3076-75 BCE. The 1955 Calendar Reform Committee notes that authorities differ on the start of the cycle.

datings.label: Dated use in Kalhana's Rajatarangini (Laukika 4224 = Shaka 1070)
datings.note: Rajatarangini 1.52 states that in the 24th year of the Laukika era 1,070 years of the Shaka era had passed, which Stein computes as Laukika 4224, 1148-49 CE.

name: Konark Sun Temple
summary: The Sun temple at Konark on the Odisha coast was built in the 13th century CE, attributed to the Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva I.
kids: The Konark temple is shaped like the giant chariot of Surya, the sun god, with huge stone wheels and stone horses pulling it.
teen: Konark's carved wheels are covered with fine sculpture, spoke by spoke.
region: Puri district, Odisha

datings.label: Reign of Narasimhadeva I

name: Madhvacharya
summary: Madhvacharya (also Anandatirtha) of the Udupi region founded the Dvaita or Tattvavada school of Vedanta, which teaches the real and permanent difference between God (Vishnu), selves and matter.
kids: Madhvacharya was a teacher from coastal Karnataka.
teen: Madhva's Dvaita Vedanta disagrees with both Shankara and Ramanuja: God, souls and matter are eternally distinct.
region: Tulu Nadu, coastal Karnataka

datings.label: Dating favoured by most scholars
Madhva tradition

name: Lalleshwari
summary: Lalleshwari (Lal Ded, Lalla) was a 14th-century Kashmiri yogini whose short verse sayings (vakh) are among the earliest works of Kashmiri literature.
kids: Lal Ded was a wise woman of Kashmir who wandered and sang short poems about finding God inside yourself.
teen: Lalla's vakhs are four-line poems in early Kashmiri.
region: Kashmir

datings.label: 14th century
datings.note: Placed in the 14th century by Kashmiri tradition and by her association with the Sufi Nund Rishi (Sheikh Nur-ud-din).

name: Kumbh Mela
summary: The Kumbha (Kumbh) Mela is a Hindu bathing festival held in a roughly twelve-year cycle, timed by the positions of Jupiter, the Sun and the Moon, at Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik-Trimbakeshwar and Ujjain.
kids: Kumbh Mela is a huge river-bathing festival held in turn at Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik and Ujjain.
teen: Timed by Jupiter's position among the zodiac signs, Kumbh Mela draws millions of pilgrims to four river cities.
region: Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik and Ujjain

datings.label: Traditional origin in the Churning of the Ocean (Chakshusha manvantara)
datings.note: Traditional accounts derive the festival from the struggle over the amrita pot after the churning, whose drops are said to have sanctified four earthly sites; the churning itself is placed in the Chakshusha manvantara before the present one.

datings.label: Xuanzang's account of Harsha's assembly at Prayag (debated antecedent)
datings.note: Popular histories cite the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang's description of a great gift-giving assembly held by King Harsha at the Prayag confluence as an early Kumbha Mela; Maclean and Lochtefeld point out that he describes a royal five-yearly assembly and mentions neither a kumbha nor a twelve-year cycle.

datings.label: Documented emergence of the twelve-year Kumbha cycle at Haridwar and its spread
datings.note: Lochtefeld traces the twelve-year Kumbha at Haridwar, timed by Jupiter in Aquarius, through records from the late 17th century; Maclean documents how the Prayag Magh Mela came to be called a Kumbh Mela during the 19th century under colonial administration.

datings.label: UNESCO inscription on the Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage
datings.note: Inscribed by the UNESCO Intergovernmental Committee for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2017.

name: Fixture extent
summary: Test data for the map snapshots: an extent outline, not an archive entry.
